text: The BRDs (Program v4, Epic 1 v4, Epic 2 v2) and the P7 functional and technical specifications are treated as the approved baseline for this PRD. No governance signature, Product Owner decision or FDA decision exists in the source documents, so the PRD is issued with status Draft and its approval table is left empty.
why: The playbook preconditions require a BRD whose status is Approved with a Product Owner decision, and the D-RCV-60 overlay forbids waiting for approval. Without this assumption the run would stop and the P7 requirement set would stay unrecorded.
read: Business Requirements Program v4 document control; Business Requirements Epic 1 v4 document control; Business Requirements Epic 2 v2 document control; FSD P7 v3 document control (Status: In review); TSD P7 v2 document control (Status: In review)
applied_in: Front matter (status: Draft); section 1.1; section 13; section 13.1
confirm: Product owner and the FDA at the requirements approval gate
impact: A different baseline version changes the requirement text this PRD quotes, not its structure; the capabilities, requirements and acceptance criteria keep their identifiers and their trace to REQ-DRI-nnn and REQ-APD-nnn.

text: Where two sources disagree about who owns a behaviour, a table or an operation, the Microservice Ownership Map v1 ruling is followed and the R-PREC precedence of the Template and Rules is applied to the sources themselves. The loser is recorded as a gap row and the PRD states the owner it uses.
why: Architecture v5, the API Specification, the P3, P4 and P7 technical specifications and the P7 functional specification disagree on several P7 items, and a PRD that stayed silent would leave a reader unable to tell which owner applies.
read: Template and Rules v1 R3 (source precedence and default rulings) and R5.5; Microservice Ownership Map v1 rulings with ASM-A6-tables-1, ASM-A6-tables-3, ASM-A6-tables-4 and ASM-A6-api-3
gap: CG-B-REQ-PRD-P7-1; CG-B-REQ-PRD-P7-2; CG-B-REQ-PRD-P7-3; CG-B-REQ-PRD-P7-4; CG-B-REQ-PRD-P7-5; CG-B-REQ-PRD-P7-12
confirm: Solution architect at the service contract review
impact: If a ruling is reversed, the affected capability moves back into this PRD as a requirement and out of the dependency list; the identifiers of the remaining capabilities do not change.

text: rwb-source-data owns the one interaction ledger: its table, write path, deduplication, ordered read and retention class. This service owns the decision ledger only, and the case timeline is served by rwb-case over the ledger contract.
why: The P7 functional specification builds ten ledger features that the R-PREC default ruling and DP-18 give to rwb-source-data, and the P1 PRD already carries them as CAP-P1-012 with FR-P1-029 and FR-P1-030. Building them here as well would create a second authoritative case history.
read: Template and Rules v1 R3 default ruling and R5.5 DP-18; Microservice Ownership Map v1 ruling 'Ledger and intake rule stay with P1 rwb-source-data' with ASM-A6-tables-1; Arch v5 slides 20 and 41; P1 PRD CAP-P1-012
confirm: Solution architect with the rwb-source-data and rwb-case contract owners
impact: Reversing it adds ten features and fourteen requirements to this PRD and removes them from the P1 PRD, and moves the ledger table, its retention class and its read API between two services.

text: There is no data lake and no Power BI connection. The central ledger is fed continuously from the decision-record topic, JOB-13 keeps its ID with continuous ingest and no Temporal Schedule, and reporting reads DecisionRecorded into rwb-reporting.
why: REQ-DRI-009, FEAT-DRI-06 and the JOB-13 copy assume a store that Architecture v5 removes, and a PRD that kept the copy would create a backlog item for removed infrastructure.
read: Arch v5 slides 20, 28, 37 and 44 (JOB-13 'ingest is continuous (Kafka)'); ADR-018; Template and Rules v1 R5.5 DP-17; Microservice Ownership Map v1 (JOB-13 replacement 'no Temporal Schedule')
confirm: Solution architect with the reporting and BI analyst
impact: Reversing it restores one capability, one requirement and its acceptance criteria, and adds a lake copy and a reconciliation check to the wave 1 slice.

text: Notice generation, letter template management, the template catalog with merge fields and proof of delivery from WIN belong to rwb-comms, with rwb-document for the document and rwb-integration for the WIN file. This service keeps only the approval of a D7.1 notice and the recording of the template version on the approval.
why: Four P7 features build the communications pipeline, and the ownership map and Architecture v5 give notices and templates to rwb-comms. Keeping them here would duplicate the notice and the template version in two services.
read: FSD P7 A2.10 to A2.13; Arch v5 slides 19 and 41 (P6 notices, templates, merge fields, proof of delivery); Microservice Ownership Map v1 (notice and template to P6); Template and Rules v1 R5.5 DP-16
confirm: Business lead with Legal counsel and the rwb-comms owner
impact: Reversing it adds four features, their requirements and their acceptance criteria, and puts the template catalog and the WIN acknowledgement back into this service's wave 2 and wave 3 slices.

text: Rule governance is central in this service: authoring, at least 50 test scenarios, four-eyes approval, effective dating, one-call rollback, version audit, promotion at 00:01 and RulePackageInForce. Evaluation is local: each model has exactly one owning service that fetches it, verifies the checksum and swaps it atomically.
why: Architecture v5 splits governance from evaluation and gives the registry to P7 while two other technical specifications claim the tables, so the PRD must state which half is this service's and which half is the owning service's.
read: Arch v5 slides 14, 27 and 41; Temporal and Drools Design v1 slide 15 and T4; ADR-017; Template and Rules v1 R5.5 DP-04; Microservice Ownership Map v1 ruling with ASM-A6-tables-3 and ASM-A6-api-3
confirm: Solution architect with the center of excellence analyst
impact: Reversing the governance half moves four tables and nine operations out of this service; reversing the evaluation half moves rule evaluation back in and contradicts the no-shared-rule-server constraint.

text: The delegation of authority table is rwb-access's. This service reads a limit through the access contract at the moment of the decision, records the delegation row ID and the limit version on the approval, and loads and approves no limit file.
why: The P7 functional specification builds the limit load, approval and rollback here, while the ownership ruling gives the table to rwb-access and Architecture v5 gives this service only an outbound read of the limits.
read: Arch v5 slide 14 (P7 OUT 'REST Access: DoA limits'); Microservice Ownership Map v1 ruling 'The DoA table is P4 rwb-access' with ASM-A6-tables-4; TSD P7 T3.3
confirm: Risk and model risk officer with the rwb-access owner
impact: Reversing it adds the limit load, its validations and its refusal messages to this service, and moves five acceptance criteria from the access PRD.

text: The completeness target for a decision record reaching the ledger is read as the five minutes of Architecture v5, with the gap alert raised at the same threshold, and the strict-mode acknowledgement is bounded by a reference-data wait value.
why: Architecture v5 states five minutes and the BRD and FSD state no value, so the PRD needs one read to size the ingest and to write a testable criterion, and it must not invent a different number.
read: Arch v5 slides 20 and 28; FSD P7 A2.5 and A2.25; BRD Program v4 NFR-033 to NFR-035
confirm: Solution architect with the platform administrator at the ADR-022 sign-off
impact: A different threshold changes one requirement, one criterion and the alert configuration; the ingest design and the capability list are unchanged.

text: A retention class is required for every decision record class and every ledger entry class, and the periods themselves stay open under DL26. The service runs no archive of its own and keeps the seal for the class period once set.
why: NFR-030 and NFR-075 are open, and a PRD that stated a period would invent a compliance value, while a PRD that stated nothing would leave the store with no declared class.
read: BRD Program v4 NFR-030 and NFR-075 (Open, DL26); FSD P7 A2.1 and A2.27; Arch v5 slide 28
impact: When the periods are set, the class gains a value and one disposal test is added; no requirement identifier changes.

text: The DecisionRecorded event carries a contract version owned by the platform event library, and this service records that version on the ledger entry and sends an unknown version to the dead-letter topic.
why: Nineteen producers share one topic and one ledger, and neither the event nor the field list says which contract a producer used, so the consumer needs a version to stay safe as producers evolve.
read: Arch v5 slides 28 and 42; TSD P7 T3.1; Template and Rules v1 R5.5 DP-09 and DP-14
confirm: Platform event library owner with the solution architect
impact: Without it, a producer change becomes a coordinated release across 19 services and the ledger holds mixed shapes without a marker.

text: rwb-case owns the case state machine and sets the Waiting approval state on ApprovalRequested (EV-09); this service raises no case task and writes only rwb_decision.
why: The FSD criteria require the case status to move on routing while the case state, the queues and the tasks are rwb-case's, and one writer of the case state keeps the state machine coherent.
read: Arch v5 slides 14 and 41; Microservice Ownership Map v1 (case and task to P3); FSD P7 AC-P7-015-01 and A2.16; TSD P7 T4
confirm: Solution architect with the rwb-case contract owner
impact: If instead this service calls the case operation, one extra dependency and one extra failure path enter the approval slice, and the case state has two writers.

text: The registry accepts an XLS decision table and a DMN 1.6 decision model as two package formats on one Drools runtime. A package version names its format, and a conversion is a version change with its own test evidence.
why: Architecture v5 proposes DMN while today's packages are XLS on the same runtime, and the registry contract, the load checks and the model fetch depend on which formats are accepted.
read: Arch v5 slides 27 and 33; Temporal and Drools Design v1 T4; ADR-012; ADR-017
confirm: Center of excellence analyst with the solution architect
impact: A single-format registry removes the conversion path from the load checks and narrows the wave 2 rule package slice; the requirement identifiers are unchanged.

text: Committee members present and their votes are carried in the approval terms structure until the field list is agreed, and the decision-log entry records the committee's outcome and its approver.
why: REQ-APD-008 and SCR-12 need the members and the votes, and the field list has neither, so an interim place to hold them keeps the Epic 4 slice buildable without inventing columns.
read: BRD Program v4 REQ-APD-008; FSD P7 Screens SCR-12 and A2.16; TSD P7 T3.1
confirm: Business lead with the center of excellence analyst before Epic 4
impact: If the structure is replaced by child tables, the approval table gains two tables and the population query gains a join; the capability and requirement identifiers are unchanged.

text: The four P7 screens are composed by gateway-bff from this service's operations. This service publishes the queue item, the decision detail, the committee pack and the search result contracts and owns their states, not the screen build.
why: DP-19 and the edge ruling put every screen behind gateway-bff while the FSD attributes four screens to the module, and the slice cannot be estimated while both readings stand.
read: Template and Rules v1 R5.5 DP-19; Arch v5 slides 19 and 41; FSD P7 Screens; TSD P7 appendix T-A
confirm: Solution architect with the platform edge owner
impact: If this service builds the screens, four screen stories move into the service epic and the wave 2 slice grows; the operations and the requirements are unchanged.
